chat.text: how many minions are doing one screenshot analysis? having one find the page(s) and launch the tool is fine, and another N to take N prompts/approaches, fine. but shouldn't those, who have already seen the image, replied with a description of the problems (and solutions?) be the one to recommend fixes? shouldn't each recommendation be easily translated to a fix? how are you sure it doesn't work? where can i see this whole process (image -> feedback -> suggested CSS fixes)? what did you mean about quoting the files back? maybe it's just telling you what it thinks it should be, which is often what it says (or close) in the CSS? that's why, getting an "increase" or "decrease" recommendation first might be better? then, when it looks up the actual code, it can apply a change? please clarify this. also, your responses during these running sessions 1) take a while to respond and 2) get buried in this vs code sidebar chat... we need a better way to chat that doesn't get buried. why are you sleeping?

**One minion per screenshot** — a fresh `claude -p` session per image; turn 2 (the CSS ask) resumes that same session, so the seat that saw the image recommends the fix. The gate used three seats per image + one Opus referee.

**Not 'doesn't work' — 'not ready', n=6.** Turn 2 wrote a decl for 6 of 74 findings; for 68 it read the CSS and answered 'intentional / markup' — *quoting the files back* = retracting its own turn-1 finding. `broken` findings scored 0.60 right, all 0.50. See the chain: [vision-fixes run](/framework/ext/DesignTool/vision/?run=/framework/ai/2026-08-17/vision-fixes/) (image → prose → fix line → decl chip + rung → $ per turn) and [quality.md](/framework/ai/2026-08-17/vision-fixes/quality.md).

**Direction first — yes.** Next experiment: `fix` = direction + property, then turn 2 must map every one to a delta given the code; referee on 30+ decls.

**Sleeping was a wrong call** — session 39% at 70% elapsed is under the line; restarting: full-corpus re-measure, the `wide` Before/After, the directional-fix experiment.

Plain English: turn 1 lists findings (what looks wrong) + a direction (increase/decrease what); turn 2, same session, reads the CSS and writes a decl (a CSS declaration) or retracts. Numbers = share the referee judged right: findings 0.62→0.30 (about half of what it points at is taste/wrong; the drop is a stricter referee), directions 0.93 (it knows which way to push), decls 0.25 (1 in 4 CSS changes right, and it wrote few), retracts 0.75 (good at dropping false alarms). Shape to keep: a pointer, not a fixer; an Opus or you reads the code and decides.
